newsitem.title: USA: Most IMM currencies close lower, marks hit bottom.
newsitem.headline: Most IMM currencies close lower, marks hit bottom.

text.p: IMM currency futures ended lower, with September marks sliding to a fresh contract low as the dollar and British pound soared to multi-year highs versus the mark in the spot market.
Dollar/mark climbed to a 41-month high of 1.7617 and sterling/mark reached a six-year high of 2.9758.

Weak German economic fundamentals and the outlook for a soft single European currency combined with steady demand for dollars by overseas investors favoring U.S. assets to hurt the mark, traders and analysts said.
September Swiss franc futures also fell, but held above support at last week's four-month low of $0.06842 and the contract low of $0.06835.

Worries that the German and Swiss central banks could move to sell some of their gold reserves after Australia's central bank announced last week it had sold gold contributed to the pressure on the European currencies, analysts said.
Meanwhile, spot sterling resumed its uptrend on stronger than expected U.K. June retail price data that reinforced expectations of a rate hike in that country.
The Bank of England's policy committee meets Wednesday and Thursday, and some analysts expect a 50 basis point rate rise. Official British interest rates now stand at 6.5 percent.

The U.K. retail price data showed underlying inflation excluding mortgage payments rose to a 2.7 percent annualized rate in June from 2.5 percent in May. The headline retail price index climbed to 2.9 percent year on year from 2.7 percent the previous month.
After an early rise, sterling futures turned lower in a light-volume profit-taking setback, traders said.
Yen futures ended nearly steady with the previous settlement after early gains faded ahead of the 2350 GMT release of May Japanese current account data.
Analysts expect the current account to show a growing surplus after the 20-day June trade surplus was reported up sharply.

Overnight comments from Eisuke Sakakibara, Japan's director general of the International Finance Bureau of the Ministry of Finance, helped deflate the yen, analysts said. Sakakibara repeated that Japan would not use foreign exchange rates as a trade tool.

September yen ended down $0.000003 at $0.008953, marks down $0.0032 at $0.5708, Swiss francs down $0.0028 at $0.6879, sterling down $0.0020 at $1.6854, Canadian dollars up $0.0010 at $0.7304, Australian dollars up $0.0026 at $0.7472 and Mexican pesos up $0.000375 at $0.123275. ((Chicago Derivatives desk 312-408-8750))
